utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 14th of May, 2008. My greetings to Mr. Scott and his colleague. My greetings to the witness, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the other people helping us out. The examination in chief is going to continue. Apparently, Mr. Karnavas, you still have one hour based on the calculations of the court deputy. Thank you. You have the floor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday there was quite a bit of a discussion concerning a couple of -- the decree and then the decision. The decision I'm speaking of is 1D 02638. We're not going to refer to that immediately but that's the one and we talked a little bit about who was a refugee. Now, you had indicated yesterday that it was on the basis of this particular decision in the previous decree that the refugees, be they Croats or Muslims or others, were being provided protection in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of -- and there was some questions from the Bench and so I thought it might be rather illustrative if we could look at 1D 01581, 1581. You have it in front of you. It's a separate sheet of paper. We see this is a -- this is already, Your Honours, in evidence. It was introduced, as I understand it, when we had Ms. Krajsek here, also it was on the list up until Monday when we tried to streamline the -- our case in keeping with your instructions. We thought we might be able to do this in three hours. In any event, if we look at this document, 1D 01581, dated 6 April 1994, and I would ask everyone to focus their attention on the very first paragraph. If you look at the second sentence in that paragraph, it says, "We are applying the same principles that we have been applied to the refugees in the Republic of Croatia as soon as the conditions for return, primarily safety are created somewhere, the refugee status for persons from that area is revoked and their return made possible, as well as the return of these persons who had decided to return of their own accord." Then we see in parentheses, "(See Law on the Status of Expelled Persons and Refugees, Article 9, paragraphs 1 and 2, Official Gazette number 96/93." Now, if we could go, with that in mind, if we could go to Articles -- to Article 9 in the decision, 1D 02638, the decision, the law itself. If you go to that. Look at Article 9. If you could tell us whether what Dr. Rebic is referring to is this particular Article, paragraphs 1 and 2. And while you're looking it up for the Trial Chamber's benefit, this can be found on the internet, this law, the Gazette actually, and the one that we have here before us is indeed 96/93. Now, is that what you were referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the decision or the letter by Mr. Rebic confirms what I was saying yesterday that both the decree and the law were consistently applied to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Furthermore, I would perhaps like to add something that we didn't mention yesterday. As a member of the United Nations, Croatia was also applying the UN Convention on the Rights of Refugees, dated 1951. When it became a member, Croatia undertook an obligation to consistently apply all of the UN conventions as well as the later protocol on the implementation of that particular convention. As far as I can tell, the documents have not been included anywhere so far. Therefore, this is not only about a consistent application of domestic legislation but rather also about the application of international laws, in this case, the rights of the refugees in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. You anticipated my next question. Let me make sure that we're thoroughly satisfied with what I'm showing you. Is what Dr. Rebic pointed out, this particular Law on the Status of Expelled Persons and Refugees, Article 9, paragraphs 1 and 2, is that what is being referred to in the decision which is 1D 02638?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if the Court wishes, I have the web site for the Official Gazette we can put it on the ELMO if that's necessary. I do have it here to make it part of the record. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. I have a question, related question for you but I'm using this document to tackle it. In this document, 1D 1581, signed by Dr. Rebic, on page 2, penultimate paragraph in the English version, it is said that nobody can return because their houses were destroyed and so on and so forth. Last time, you were not here, Dr. Prlic made a statement and at one point in time he said this and this sort of puzzled me. I was waiting for a witness to come in order to check this. Dr. Prlic told us that with regard to the ownership of apartments, there was some kind of social right. I was under the impression that Yugoslavia, which initially was a country with a communist system, there was no ownership right as such. It was the state that would allocate apartments and dwellings to individuals who would occupy it but it was social ownership, and because of what Dr. Prlic said, I was under the impression that in the Republic of Croatia, this system was somewhat different. I believe, I understood that the Croats were owners of their apartments. Could you shed some light on this as to the system that was in place before the breakdown of Yugoslavia? You, for instance, were you the owner of your apartment because you had some deed of ownership that was authenticated by a notary public or was a social ownership, collective ownership, that you were given your apartment by the municipality, you could occupy it and the municipality could, in turn, give that apartment to somebody else and then when the state of Yugoslavia broke down, states turned into liberal economy and market economy and there was ownership for individuals. Could you shed some light on the issue of ownership of an apartment that can apply to displaced persons or to refugees equally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm privy to the inner workings of this particular matter in Croatia as well as in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, there was socially-owned property. There was also private property; private property, however, was not to exceed some very strict limits. People had the right to actually own flats and homes. That was my case as well. My parents owned a house. There were flats, for example, that were allocated by a municipal body, a company or an institution. Such flats would remain socially owned, as they say. A family or a person would be granted the right to use that flat, but under a certain set of conditions. If there was a failure on the part of this person or family to comply with these conditions, the authorities allocating the flat were free to simply take the flat away from that person or family and allocate it to someone else. As far as I know, however, socially-owned property to all practical intents was viewed and dealt with in the same way as any other form of property because that was what people did in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next -- let's go on to the next document, 1D 02606, and you'll see there are several pages to this particular document. If you could please take a look at it first, especially the copies in the original language, in Croatian. My first question would be: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a table. It is a report or a partial report on how and when and where the Office for Refugees was ordering and distributing heaters. Preparations were underway for the winter season and obviously one needed to get a certain amount of heaters in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could we get a date -- I have not been able to find a date on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't finished with my direct examination. I haven't laid a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. You were going to provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to snap but, I mean, we're professionals around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, when one shows a witness a document or provides a document to a party, usually the information about date is provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How do you recognise this document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would receive reports such as this one, and that's why I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to answer the Prosecution's question: Do you know when this document was generated? And I don't want to lead you but if you look at it closely, you'll see some dates on the document as far as when certain incidents are reported. It's the European version of putting down the dates so maybe that might cause some confusion.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did this just on the eve of winter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's just go to the next -- by the way, if we just look at the one document, we can see the date, 1992, rather very clearly. You have a listing, this would be on -- I believe it's the fourth page. You see several hotels that are being mentioned. Can you tell us where are these locations?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These facilities, all of them, are somewhere along the coast. The Split area, the Makarska area, with the exception of a single one that happens to be in the Zagreb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you flip to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just for precision -- thank you for the precision's sake, there is a mistake in the translation. The entry for -- under number 9 for Gortan says 4 January 1992, which is amazing because all the rest is referring to winter 1992, 1993, and if you look at the Croatian version then you see that it should read 1993. I think it's just a bit awkward and I think we want everything to be precise and correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you go to the next page, where it says, "Adaptation of facilities, UNHCR." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see all these dates are 1992. And if you look under number 8, it says "Gasinci." Is that the island?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Gasinci is not an island; it's a refugee centre near Djakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this shows, however, is that it was the UNHCR that made over a former military officers's HQ into a refugee centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the one that Azra Krajsek was saying that the weapons were pointed at, is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, this is -- I'm going to object to that for this kind of commentary. The witness doesn't know that except what Mr. Karnavas tells him, so he has no -- this witness has no information about what did or didn't happen. So, Your Honour, I'm going to make the point. This is why I'm constantly on my feet about commentary, comments, arguments by counsel, characterizations. It's not necessary and it's not done properly in the common law system. You ask a question. This is direct examination, cannot be leading. You ask an open-ended, non-leading, non-suggestive question. That's all we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question. We'll see the document next week when we have our next witness because there is -- there are documents that were in the packet that we had prepared to show to this gentleman but next week we will see complaints from Krajsek and Turkovic that weapons were being pointed at that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, isn't that a bit of a strange argument? What does what happens next week to do with how you now question this witness? And in fact, you have asked him to comment on what another witness has said. He hasn't, to my knowledge, been present when the other witness deposed, I don't think whether he saw the transcript. I think the Prosecution -- the objection must be sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all, let me just respond. I wasn't making an argument, I was responding to the Prosecution. Secondly, yesterday, we discussed this incident. Yesterday, I pointed to portions of the transcript from the witness. He had indicated yesterday that at that particular camp which had a UNHCR centre, under no circumstances, to his knowledge when he visited it, and mind you he's up there until 1993 in his position, were any weapons being pointed. Now we see a date 1992. My whole point is that because there are complaints that these two particular centres of which those are the only two out of nearly 600 that there are complaints, we have as of 1992 people being stored over there. Now who are the displaced persons or refugees? Where are they coming from on this particular date? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, fortunately we have a continuation of the problem. Now Mr. Karnavas is testifying when he says of 600 centres there were only two complaints. We don't know that. There's no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday there was evidence there were 596.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as far as this witness knows, which he wasn't even there between March 1993 and late 1995, as far as he knows -- as far as I know, nothing ever happened in Croatia. I wasn't there. As far as I know. As far as this witness knows, he knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have to say something on this issue. The issue you raise is as follows: There is some accommodation for refugees. Apparently these premises were premises where senior officers were accommodated previously, so there was a military connotation to the premises. Based on that, it may be that there were weapons, guns on the premises. I don't know. And based on that, you try to clarify what another witness may have said. Two things are here an issue. In my country, a defence counsel could tell a witness the following: Witness, another witness stated that in this location, there were guns directed against the refugee camp and the witness could agree or disagree. This is something that can be done. A question that can be asked. In a common law system, according to Mr. Scott, that is not done. I note that. However, in the system -- a mixed system as applied in this Tribunal, you may find a mixture of both system, both systems and sometimes they collide and that causes procedural incidents. This is what I wanted to say but since you're moving on to another subject, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, but just to make sure. I don't agree with Mr. Scott's insinuation that this is improper direct examination. It may be where he comes from but where I come from, I'm perfectly capable of referring to what another witness has indicated and asking the witness to comment if I can establish that that witness has a basis, they have a factual basis to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you visited Gasinci?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time, if you look at the date, this is 2/12/92, could you please tell us whether there were any displaced persons or refugees staying at that location?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could we have the dates of Mr. -- Dr. Zoric's visits to the place, if we're talking about visits in 1991, 1992. I'm quite serious about this. We need to know a date. What happened in 1991 can be completely irrelevant to what happens in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've indicated already that the gentleman worked in that capacity. When he visited a particular location is absolutely irrelevant. What's relevant is: During that period when he was working did he know whether people were housed over there? That's the foundational question. So I don't see why the Prosecution is getting so excited. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think here you're right, Mr. Karnavas, and I would overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So do you know, based on your position, whether -- who was there, if anybody, at that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Look at the date, Mr. Scott, please. I know that this is European style of -- look at it, it's 2.12.92. You're wearing your glasses, you must be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I reject this kind of personal commentary. This is not required, this is not called for. It is just attacks on counsel and the Court, with all respect, should not allow this and Mr. Karnavas should be admonished. Now, I'm looking at the -- I don't have a translated document in front of me. Yes, I can read the date. If counsel says -- excuse me, Your Honour, let me make my record. If counsel says, if counsel says that all he's referring to is that particular date -- in December 1992, and that's all we're talking about because sometimes it's not clear, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But here it was absolutely clear, counsel has started off his question by referring to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I am mistaken I stand corrected. I'm not perfect but I did not understand that going into it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was anybody staying in that location, to your knowledge, back then; and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both refugees and displaced persons at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Karnavas please try to speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us how often you have visited this particular location on or about that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four times, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see how the facility was being set up and what exactly was going on. It was my job to tour places that like that to see whether they were operating properly. Again, I must point out that there were no weapons being kept there. The fact that the facility had been used by senior officers of the former army doesn't necessarily mean that they left any weapons behind. That particular army never left a single weapon behind, at least that much is generally known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, and at the risk of being criticised by the Court again, I'm sorry but I'm back to my saying -- so when he says he visited it three or four times, during what period are we talking about? During December 1992, that time, or throughout a three- or four- or five-year period, or -- I'm sorry, but I'm going to ask for the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, so you -- well, I would find it difficult to say in which month I was in which location 15 years ago, but maybe you have a better memory than I do. Could you more or less tell us when you visited the facility or are you not in a position to do so, which I would understand perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to be particularly specific about dates but it was certainly the case whenever there was something very important going on. When the larger groups arrived, when there were things to be done, or when UNHCR teams went, I would tag along. I think there was a total of maybe three or four times that I visited Gasinci in 1992, but I can't be any more specific about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just one last question about this document, you see at the very top it says, "Adaptation of facilities UNHCR." Can you tell us what exactly are these figures? What does this mean? And you may have to look at the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These figures show the dates when contracts were signed and they show how much money was spent under the terms of those contracts. They also show the amounts of money remaining and they also show the deadlines for this makeover. The UNHCR is bankrolling the whole project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I know yesterday we saw a document 1D 2609 and that was a letter of mutual intent to conclude an agreement and we saw that your office, ODPR, was to report in financial and narrative form the use of all contributions received. Now, granted this is at a latter date, this document I'm referring to right now, and it's about something slightly different but may I ask, the funds that were being received from UNHCR, was your office responsible for accounting for how that money was spent where and for what purposes?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the office was accountable for that and joint bodies decided how and on what that money is to be spent. We cooperated with the UNHCR and after the job had been done, we submitted reports on what we had done and how much money we had spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 01294, that's the next document. This refers to a Dr. Bisera Turkovic, appointed ambassador to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia, did you know this woman?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met her several times at receptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any official dealings with her while she was the ambassador, and I'm speaking now for time-frame purposes, up until the time when you were the office ODPR in 1993, that is, did you have any official meetings with her?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had very little contact with the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you have so little contact with her? I see that she was appointed in the month of January, 1993. I know that you were there until the month of March so you had the entire month of February to have contacts. And if there were refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, should she not have contacted you in order to solve these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so and that was actually part of her mandate to take care of BiH citizens but they contacted me very rarely. I met the lady once or twice. We spoke politely, introduced each other, exchanged a few courteous phrases and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to make sure, to follow up on what you had indicated yesterday. Above you was Dr. Rebic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And given his position, would it have been more likely that she or her representative would have contacted Dr. Rebic as opposed to you, you being the number two albeit you're the one handling the day-to-day affairs?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Rebic represented the office and it is natural for the representatives of foreign countries to contact him first. But if he had been approached about any activities that we should do, I would have learned about it because I would have been the one to implement that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, where was your office with respect to Dr. Rebic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karnavas speak into the microphone to the right.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sitting in the same building, he was on the first floor and I was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next document 1D 02607. 1D 02607. This is dated February 3, 1993, and again, I just want some clarification. It says, "One-time financial assistance for refugees from BiH who organised their lives independently and for their hosts." Now, can you just comment very briefly what does this mean? I know you touched upon it yesterday but we had that whole argument about whether the law applied and whether Croatia was actually taking care of refugees, Muslim refugees, but if you could look at this, could you please tell us what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction to regional offices and local offices of social welfare centres who worked with refugees about the distribution of financial assistance to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina; namely, to those refugees who lived independently rather than in collective accommodation centres but who were registered as refugees in Croatia. Those who were registered and lived in collective refugee centres had their costs covered by us; and those refugees who lived independently received financial assistance occasionally in the form of one-time financial assistance. This is for refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at just paragraph number 4, keeping in mind your testimony yesterday about the centres and then the regional office and the reporting system and keeping track of the data and updating the census, can you comment on this a little bit?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph speaks about the obligation to forward data to the centre. Dr. Kurent, at the time, was the head of the international department of our office and she closely cooperated with the UNHCR. He was sort of our minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the data would come from the centres to the regional office and then from the regional office to the head office; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go on to the next document, 1D 02283, dated 25 February 1993. We see this is a protocol on cooperation between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish logistics centres in the Republic of Croatia for the reception and distribution of humanitarian aid sent to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now my first question is: Were you aware of this protocol?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go back to the second page, we see Dr. Mate Granic, that's the individual that initially got you involved; correct? And that you were working for?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you involved in any way with implementing this protocol albeit it's now February 25th and you're only there shortly in that office in ODPR before you go and take your seat on the parliament.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, few organisations that wanted to help Bosnia-Herzegovina went there directly. It was much easier for everybody to bring the aid to Croatia and then through the cooperation of Croatian and BiH organisations or governments was that aid transported to Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, there was heavy fighting going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and many companies were reluctant to go there apart from soldiers, the UNPROFOR but civilian companies very rarely did so, only to some regions. So Sarajevo felt the need to have logistical centres in Croatia and they were set up mostly in Split and Zagreb. It was our duty according to the instructions given by government to assist them in finding warehouses and we did, at least in Zagreb, and I took part in that. We found warehousing facilities in the Zagreb International Trade Fair premises. Some existing facilities were converted into warehouses and from there, they independently organised the distribution of goods to wherever they felt necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next document, 1D 027 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. I have a follow-up question. Witness, you just said something that struck me as being very important. You talked about a document which relates to the cooperation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and it seems that centres have been put in place in order to receive refugees coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us, this system seems that it is -- it seems that it's linked to Serb or Serbian actions which seems to be responsible for the displacement of these persons which means that at least for a certain period of time, an agreement existed between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina so that Croatia receives refugees and the system worked in that way. Am I right when I say this, when I draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you're referring to this protocol, it is about logistics and we had other protocols signed about receiving and taking back refugees from and to Bosnia-Herzegovina, those are protocols between our two countries. This protocol is about the establishment of logistical centres in Croatia but such centres that would be managed by the representatives of the Sarajevo authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we understand correctly, an agreement existed between the parties so that the Sarajevo government is in charge of the implementation of these centres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this cooperation, to your knowledge, how long did it last? The two states had this agreement for how long in order to make sure that things work well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was being implemented throughout the war. Now, it's because these centres assisted in the return of these people. In an operational fashion, I believe that they were active until 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now you're saying throughout the war. I no longer follow you. Which war are you talking about? There are many wars. Would you kindly be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can be more precise. From the humanitarian aspect, there was one single war. We may be able to say that there were many wars if we look at it from different angles. I mean the war that went on until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make sure I understand you absolutely well. Do you mean that during the BiH offensive in the Lasva Valley, for instance, in Central Bosnia, while combat operations were taking place, this agreement between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia was fully operational?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As a part of the paradox that we lived through, and it was a bitter part of our work. People complained to us and there were situations, sometimes, that soldiers spent their leave with their families who were refugees and watching the news, some of them would rejoice and others would cry. And it was -- those were very hard times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to pick up on that. You said "soldiers." Where were these soldiers? Where were they from? Where would they go? I don't want to lead you, just tell us, and give us an example if you could.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers, as you know, were in the position to get weekend leave and the like and they would come from Central Bosnia or Herzegovina, mostly to Dalmatia and if they spent their weekend leaves, then it was mostly with their families who were refugees there. It was very difficult to cross lines in the war, the lines held by Serbian forces because they -- their forces were strong. But the front line between the Croatian and the Bosnian forces were soft lines so it was possible to cross them at some places and so did I. And there were situations and reports were made about that, about great emotional stress that practically in the same small town or facility, you would have people from one and the other side. But all obligations that the government had taken upon itself were being implemented. All logistical centres were functional and all aid to Bosnia-Herzegovina went through Croatia. Actually it was transported over one single bridge which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I asked you a very concrete question if you could give us a concrete answer. The question is: You said "soldiers." Are we talking about Muslim soldiers killing Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the weekdays and then going to visit their family in say Makarska during the weekend. That's a concrete example. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether those who killed others actually came to Croatia and if they came, they didn't come as soldiers, they came as citizens. But as citizens, they were admitted to Croatia freely because there was no visa regime in place with Bosnia-Herzegovina nor could it -- nor could there have been such a regime because Croatia was the immediate neighbour of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small detail that might be interesting, those soldiers who would go visit their family in Croatia, would they come wearing jeans, a suit or would they actually come wearing their military fatigues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, they couldn't come in uniforms. They could come in civilian clothes but we're talking about people from small towns or villages and everybody knows everybody else. And Central Bosnia is a small place where you can't be anonymous and it wasn't hard to recognise people if they were from the same town or village as you. Apart from that, the logistical centres were the destination of delegations and convoys, et cetera, from Bosnia-Herzegovina including military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one final question on that. When we're talk about soldiers, which particular armies are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about soldiers of the army of BiH or soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in other words, a soldier from the army of BiH could take off his uniform, go across the border, have a nice little weekend, visit the family then go back to the front line in Central Bosnia? That's what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were able to do so, not everybody, but some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go on to the next document 1D 02778, 1D 02778. If we look at the bottom, we see that this is from the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees, February 1993, Zagreb. And sir, first of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What is this document? Without going into the contents, just tell us what is it, basically?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a flyer containing information or an appeal of our office which was distributed on a regular basis to everybody willing to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus everyone's attention to paragraph number 2, especially in light of our discussion yesterday and today as far as aid to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says here, "At present, (February) there are approximately 400.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina registered in Croatia and 250.000 displaced persons (people who came from occupied or war-ravaged area in Croatia). That is to say that Croatia is responsible for the accommodation of more than 650.000 people, of which are accommodated in hotels, private homes, schools, huts, and train cars." Question: Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose for this flyer, because we see that they are requesting assistance of people to give, basically.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are asking for donations and assistance and we're trying to maintain the awareness of people that there is a need to give. Otherwise, we wouldn't have been able to bear this burden. So we were constantly raising the awareness of the general public letting them know that we must help our -- we must all help each other and help ourselves to live through this difficult period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, witness, you talked about 650.000 people or that's what the document states and it's a huge number and we see that these people were accommodated in various places, hotels, schools, and so on and so forth and even in private homes. To your knowledge, had you heard of the fact that Croatians would have accommodated in their own homes Muslims that they would have accommodated during the war? Do you have any examples to give us, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. There are many examples of this type. In towns and villages, people would receive refugees in their homes. More than half the refugees were not put up in organised camps or facilities but they were put up in the homes of Croatian citizens who were not forced to take them up. They did so of their own accord. Of course you would first admit your relatives or friends, but many people took up persons who had simply turned up and who needed help. And there are many examples of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Financially speaking, if a Croatian family was accommodating, for instance, Muslim refugees who had absolutely not a penny, they only, let's say, came with a suitcase, do you know if that Croatian family, for instance, could receive a financial aid from either the municipality or the government in order to help them to feed these Muslim refugees? Do you know if there was a system in place of social protection that existed to help these people who were accommodating these refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such families could get support if there were funds available. This assistance was not paid out regularly. There were no set dates but rather as one-time financial assistance. The system of distribution, of humanitarian aid to such families functioned rather well and those humanitarian aid mostly consisted in food and household items. Many organisations were engaged in that such as Karitas, Merhamet, the Red Cross, and other smaller organisations. Families who had put up refugees in their homes would get aid from these. The financial assistance was scarce, though, which, as a consequence, financially exhausted the host families because the overall economic situation in Croatia was by no means brilliant and there are expenses connected with housing. So that one-time financial assistance was made available to the office to distribute to these families and sometimes we would get resources from UNHCR and also distribute them to these families but that was no regular assistance. It was provided occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's in contrast to what you told us yesterday if somebody were to go to say Germany where, as I understand it, you indicated yesterday per individual would be a thousand marks a month; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Germany was a much richer country. Was and still is. There was some federal states where refugees received that type of subsidy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I bring the correction, I think the witness says up to a thousand mark which does not mean that everybody got automatically a thousand marks. Do I understand you correctly, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're shaking your head, you have to say ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go on to the next document, 1D 02626, 2626. It's dated 12 June 1998. Let me ask some preliminary questions. First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote reports such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And some of the data that's included there, at least during the period that you were there in that particular office, and we know that you went back in 1995, can you please tell us where this data came from?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary of what went on over a number of years. There are a number of different sources for this report, the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, the UNHCR, and other organisations that were working with refugees and displaced persons in Croatia at the time. This document gives you a general picture of the situation as it was. It also gives you precise statistics as to what was going on with these refugees and displaced persons in Croatia over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus on two things in this particular document, not everything -- we can all read it. If you look at footnote number one it talks about elections for BiH that were held in 1996. Can you tell us whether the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees participated in any way with the elections that were held for BiH?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first post-war elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina were held in September 1996. This was organised and monitored by the OSCE. A decision was taken that elections would be held among Bosnia's refugees living abroad as well. There was another decision to hold elections in Croatia among Bosnia's refugees. The OSCE entrusted the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons with this project. I was appointed coordinator for this whole registering procedure. All Bosnia's refugees in Croatia, all those who wanted to take part in the elections had to register first. A total of about 120.000 refugees eventually registered. I believe a total of 97.000 actually took part in the elections. I think the document actually states the exact number, 93.456 people, eventually took part in the elections. We organised and held these elections in cooperation with the OSCE. The OSCE had a permanent representative in our office and they also had dozens of monitors all over the country where elections were being held and in our office as well. There was this permanent representative of the OSCE who was in charge of monitoring the procedure on their behalf. He was from Switzerland, his name was Tobias Werler and I think he was from Basel and that's the extent of what I know about him. I don't think I've ever seen him again. It was necessary to get funding for the elections to be held and it was necessary also to get technical assistance and this is something that either we or the OSCE made sure was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as a result of your participation and your office's participation, did you ever receive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As a result of your participation and your office's participation in this election, did you ever receive any accommodation or any comments from OSCE?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then representative of the OSCE Bosnia-Herzegovina Ambassador Frowick sent a very nice letter. As a result, we were all very proud. He said something to the effect that the entire procedure was a major contribution to the growth of democracy in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was that ever published so that the world would know your office's participation in this event?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was widely publicised. It was on the news and I think he sent a separate letter to the Foreign Minister and the letter was forwarded to the media. It was on the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One quick question on this. Why was it that the embassy for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb was not entrusted with this task? Why go to the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a question for the OSCE and not for me. I do believe, however, that the embassy back then did not really have the level of organisation that an effort like this would have demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did the embassy ever complain that this particular office, the ODPR, had been unfair, had been unkind, had been uncaring to its citizens and therefore should not be entrusted with this rather important function?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no complaints like that. Quite the contrary, in fact. The embassy was one of the monitoring institutions. Parties from Bosnia-Herzegovina dispatched their own representatives to observe, since there was quite a large number of votes being cast, especially in those municipalities that wanted to go back to their ethnic make-up as it was before the war; therefore, every single vote counted. Parties also sent their leaders over to promote their own parties in major centres where refugees from staying. Those were Croat parties from Bosnia and Herzegovina or Bosnian parties from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Both ethnic groups. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to page 3, page 3, paragraph 4, the last paragraph within the section where it says, "Between the summer -- between summer 1995 and May 1996 in Croatia, about 20.000 Muslim refugees from Velika Kladusa and Cazin stayed in Krupljensko, Republic of Croatia." Then it goes on to say, "They are not included in the numbers mentioned above. The camp was closed in May 1996 when the last group of refugees moved to refugee settlements in Gasinci and Obonjan." Let's stop right there. Do you have any information regarding this particular passage?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refugees who arrived in Krupljensko were refugees from the Velika Kladusa and Cazin areas. They made two attempts to enter Croatia. There was a lot going on there and I think Abdic's forces lost out eventually. I'm not going into what was actually going on in Velika Kladusa at the time, however, much of Croatia's territory was still under occupation. It was somewhere near Karlovac that they tried to cross the front line but they were unable to, the front line separating the Croat forces from the Serb forces. As a result, they were returned to Velika Kladusa. An operation was then launched to liberate those areas. Following an operation by the BiH army taking Velika Kladusa and Cazin, the followers of Abdic, about 20.000 of them, arrived in a small village in Croatia called Krupljensko. They settled down and turned themselves into a major international problem. They refused to go back. They refused to be put up anywhere else. International organisations and our own office provided them with assistance and food. The conditions in that village were truly miserable. Nevertheless, the Republic of Croatia and Turkey along with the authorities of the newly-established Federation of B and H set up a system of police patrols that were operating throughout western Bosnia in Cazin and Velika Kladusa. In this sense, this gave the refugees a feeling of safety and made it possible for them to go back. Nevertheless, they had heard while still in the camp of several cases of revengism and refugees being killed. It was very difficult for them to take this step and decide to go back. Despite this, after months of ongoing activity by the police forces of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Turkey, about 16.000 people eventually returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. About 4.000 of those, however, categorically refused to return. We ended up allowing those 4.000 persons to remain in Gasinci and we put them up. Some of them sought asylum in third countries. Most of them, however, eventually returned to their homes in B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, where they were initially settled, was that camp that was sanctioned and operated by ODPR?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was a village. They came to that village, it was that simple, and they settled down. They put up tents that they had brought along on lorries. They built mud huts. This wasn't a very dignified kind of housing, it was just very makeshift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there complaints about this particular camp; and if so, who was complaining? And keep it brief, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dealing with this issue, I think, was the last term for Croatia to be admitted into the Council of Europe. As you well know, Croatia was eventually admitted and we dealt with the Krupljensko problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your answer adds one more complex features to the issue we're seized of. We've seen various documents with figures concerning the refugees. Initially, refugees coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina can be put into two broad categories, the Croats and the Muslims. As for the latter, on the basis of your answer, I see that there were among them Muslims who were in favour of the Croats, for instance, Abdic's troops. So there were Muslims who were pro-Croats. They were accommodated and accepted as refugees and are included into the general statistics. So that's one additional factor that we'll have to take into account and assess. With regard to your office, when you were informed of the arrival of these Muslim refugees, did you ever make a distinction between one category and the other or were they all refugees, Muslim refugees without your office making any distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't draw that type of distinction, nor indeed was it possible to draw one. I didn't think of Muslims as being pro-Croat or perhaps another kind. They were what they were, even those in western Bosnia. The history of this conflict is quite complex. I think some of those forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that, you don't need to go into that. It's very complex and every passing day gives us further evidence of that. I am interested in knowing whether there were any distinctions among Muslims. You, see, why I'm raising this issue because I have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, there was no distinction. We didn't draw one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I asked you this is that in the document, 1D 2637, first page in the English version, figures are mentioned 1.8 million refugees, 900.000 from BiH and these figures clarify things, but there is a second paragraph that says that there are people who returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This return to BiH is to be found in paragraph III of page 2, (i) in December of 1992 in Croatia, there were 371.319 refugees. In the following paragraph, the situation prevailing in May 1993 is described when they registered 271.096 refugees from BiH that were granted the status of refugees and that's where things get interesting in my view. It is said that many went to European countries and there is a small group that was not granted that status, apparently. That group of people returned to BiH. That's what I'm interested in. On the basis of this paragraph, one could have proof that individuals came to Croatia in order to be granted the status of refugees and then they returned back to BiH. It's written in this document. You could not have drafted this document because it was drafted in 1998. It may be that you were informed of this, but I am interested in the situation in May. This document says that Muslims returned to BiH. Were you aware of this? It may be that you were no longer in the office in May, but you were an MP so as an MP, in theory, you must be informed of various things. Did you know that Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina arrived in Croatia to return later to BiH as seems to be indicated by this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Your Honour, when reports talk about the numbers of refugees that were put up in Croatia at a given point in time, the reference is only to those who were in Croatia at this precise point in time. It doesn't necessarily mean there weren't any other refugees there but they'd either left for third countries or had returned to BH. We handled nearly a million people through our office in different ways who came, left, went elsewhere, or perhaps returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. At times, there were as many as 200 to 300.000 people at a time. Some came, some left, some went back to Bosnia and Herzegovina and then back to Croatia and then were granted status as refugees again. Between 1993 and 1995, and this might strike one as petty and not enough, but we worked with humanitarian workers, representatives of various organisations and so on and so forth, we managed to have about 5.000 people returned to B and H. This may seem as little but it was a huge success. In 1993, we started cooperating with the German authorities in terms of bringing people back. If you look at the statistics in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout, you will realise that there were a number of towns from which we, in Croatia, and the countries all over Europe were receiving refugees all the time such as Zenica, for example. These cities would provide their own figures on the numbers of refugees that they were facing at a given point in time. There was a lot of migration. People were moving about a lot, but between 1993 and 1995, in particular, people started returning more and more. Sometime in March 1995, the respective governments of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Office For Refugees on the one hand and the directorate from Mostar on the other signed a protocol on the return of refugees and displaced persons, there was an international tripartite agreement also that was later to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is an important issue, I'm going to be more specific. I'm interested in the year 1993 and the beginning of 1994, in that period. You have just said that between 1993 and 1995, 5.000 people returned to BiH, fine. Could you be more specific in your answers? Among these 5.000 individuals in that period from 1993 to beginning of 1994, could it be that some of them returned to Herzegovina, that is, to the areas that were controlled by the HVO? It's very important for us to know that. Could it be, as far as you know, that Muslims who returned to the territory that was controlled by the HVO in 1993 and early 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and there were Muslims among the people who returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, and if the Chamber will allow me. In looking at the information and just so the record is not confused, there's -- these numbers did not distinguish between Croats and Muslims, where it says, "5.000 people from BiH returned." We don't know if they were 5.000 Croats or 5.000 something else or a mixture. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to specify this. My question was very, very specific. It dealt only with Muslims who may have returned to BiH to areas controlled by the HVO in 1993, early 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Muslim refugees, too, who returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you absolutely certain of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you have a few minutes left before the break and you don't have much time left anyway, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have enough to conclude, Your Honour, but perhaps it might be better to just take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you'd rather we took the break now? We'll have a break. In the meantime, the court deputy is going to tell us how many minutes or seconds you have left and then when we resume, you will be able to proceed to finish. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have nine more minutes, or 450 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go back to the document that we were on, just one technical question or two to finish it up. 1D 02626, going back to paragraph 4 which is on page 3. You had indicated that there were about 4.000 persons that refused to go back to BiH and they had to be resettled, and they went to Gasinci and Obonjan. So my next question is who moved them?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ODPR moved them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we talked earlier about the fact that there were elections. Were they still there when the elections took place?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were there voting booths over there or were people allowed to go to various centres to vote? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Gasinci, there was a polling station because there were people from Bosnia-Herzegovina there. Whoever was there and was registered and wanted to vote could do so at Gasinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move on to something else. You had indicated in 1993, sometime in March, you became a member of parliament and we know that as of March 1993 and thereafter, and to some parts of 1994, there were some clashes between the army of BiH and the HVO and we have refugees from both sides coming into Croatia. My question is this: While you were a member of parliament, do you ever recall having any discussions and the government passing any proposals or the parliament, to limit the entry of Muslim refugees into Croatia or to limit the assistance that they would be receiving once into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parliament never passed such decisions, but I know that the government turned to the international community requesting assistance and that many governments reacted and notified us of their quotas, say, the number of refugees they would accept. Germany was willing to put up the greatest number of refugees, some countries were unwilling to accept any, and some Islamic countries such as Malaysia, Sudan, Turkey and others were also willing to accept some. There were also offers saying we were ready to accept so and so many in this country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Recognising the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Central Bosnia in particular, where you indicated that refugees that were both Croat and Muslim coming there, were there any efforts to somehow discriminate against the Muslim refugees that were coming in?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry but -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That he's aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can't get my microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I appreciate Mr. Karnavas says that he's aware of but that's an extremely broad question and that he's aware of. I mean as a member of parliament not involved with these issues on a daily basis, is he aware of? And I mean, again, as I mentioned earlier this morning that's like asking anyone, you know, did Joe wear a blue shirt yesterday that you are aware of? Well, I'm not aware of it but that doesn't mean anything. I think there has to be some specification here and some indication of personal knowledge other than a wild guess as, well, I never heard of anything. I mean, was he involved in these issues? Was he sitting on a committee? Was there a particular report? During this entire period, we're talking about a year's -- a long period of time, is he aware of anything by anyone, anywhere in the Croatian government to discriminate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll ask a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From March 1993 until the time that you go back to the ODPR, were you aware of what was happening in Croatia with respect to the refugees and displaced persons? We'll go step-by-step, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not trying to be difficult. I'm really not. But I do have to make a fair record here and I am a party to this as much as anybody else. What does that mean? "Aware of what was happening in Croatia?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have to go step-by step. First, if he says no then that's the end of the series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course he's going to say presumably, anyone who read the newspaper on a daily basis is going to say, Well, I had some awareness of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will refocus it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any discussions in parliament with respect to the refugees and displaced persons keeping in mind that you've indicated that there were budgetary constraints and also there was a budget with respect to the financing of the various centres? So were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were debates in parliament about these issues. There were public -- there was public debate, there were political debates and some people took part in them, so did I sometimes. It was the goal of all of us to appease the situation, to end the conflict and to create the conditions for the people to return to their homes. These positions were uttered publicly and officially asserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during the course of these proceedings, we've been making a record and at which point I asked concretely on the record for the Prosecutor to tell us whether it was in his opinion whether the government of Croatia, and by that I meant the state of Croatia, whether they were being charged with a failure to provide adequate assistance to the refugees and whether Mr. Rebic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise by virtue of his occupation. That could be found on page 20.009, so 20.009. Mr. Scott responded as follows on the following page, 20.010 starting with line 6, he says, "I'll respond directly. Yes, that is part of the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina and from Herceg-Bosna area. This was part of a system as charged in the indictment to move Muslims out of Herceg-Bosna and it was done any number of ways. One of those ways was to move them either at least temporarily into Croatia and either to abandon them there which may have come up further in parts or -- of the testimony of this witness or to move them on to other countries but not to return them to Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, based on that, to your understanding, based on your involvement both when you were in that office up until 1993 and thereafter 1995, but more specifically while you were out of the office but a member of the parliament, to your understanding was there a concerted effort on the state of Croatia or officials of the state of Croatia such as Mr. Rebic to turn Croatia into some sort of a transit centre to force Muslim refugees outside to third countries, the further away, that is, so they couldn't go back -- go back to their homelands and thus ethnically cleansing the area. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, do I understand Dr. Zoric now to be speaking on behalf of every person, every official, every authority in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a joint criminal enterprise. This is the office that is responsible for these refugees. You have Dr. Rebic who is at the top. This gentleman was second in command. As I understand from all the objections, and I can only guesstimate but from all the objections, it's the Prosecution's argument that sometime when this gentleman was outside of that office, when the events are happening in Central Bosnia, it is at that point at least with respect to ODPR that they become a member of the joint criminal enterprise and thus Dr. Rebic or others may be either aiding and abetting the crimes or are members of or are the physical perpetrators, one of those three. Those are the three options. Now, it is the Prosecution's argument that Croatia is turned into a transit centre. I'm asking this gentleman because if this is an argument, if this is an office of the government of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if this gentleman is a member of the parliament, and if it's being budgeted, clearly something must be aware of what is happening. Dr. Rebic could not be acting on his own. Is he getting -- we're going to see the gentleman, but to his knowledge, to his knowledge, is this office part of the joint criminal enterprise as a result of it being an agency of the state of -- the Republic of Croatia. I mean that's the danger of this joint criminal enterprise. But we have -- you know and this is -- this is the alleged JCE and of course we have Mr. Scott's words, so I'm asking this gentleman, being aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, sir, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can. I think that drawing conclusions about ethnic cleansing and linking that to the activities of the ODPR would be wrong. I will give a number of reasons. Firstly, in our documents, as far as I can see, we can see complaints from Bosnia-Herzegovina that the ODPR did not grant people the right to enter Croatia in -- every time. So if you are ethnically cleansing then why don't you let people enter your country? Why keep them where they were? Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, the ODPR was in no position to send anyone to a third country without the consent of the person in question and the country in question. And so the -- if we were to make this conclusion, this would be very discriminatory towards the governments of Germany, the Netherlands or Turkey, Egypt, Sudan, Iran or Malaysia which countries also accepted refugees. All transportation, all departures of these refugees were organised at an international level and the international community at the time operated in Zagreb through another organisation, the International Organisation for Migrations so that many countries, including the USA, Canada, Australia and others, through that organisation, also accepted people from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do not see how Dr. Rebic could have influenced or exerted influence on the Canadian government to set a quota or any other government, for that matter, or a quota saying how many people they would accept. That was not our job. What I would like to say is that throughout the time people were received in Croatia and people left for third countries, there was also the reverse direction, albeit limited, of return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in 1995 when five European countries joined the German-Croatian agreement on the return of refugees through Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Starting from March that year, this was done in accordance with the protocol and the agreement signed by the government in Sarajevo and the government in Zagreb. In March, I was not yet in the office, but later on that year, I was and saw the agreement and implemented it for two years. It was through that office that people returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina and that can, by no means be called ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, sir. Now, I misspoke on page 41, Your Honours, I believe it was line 2, I said the government of BiH, it should have been the government of Croatia, just to correct that, to correct myself, that is. All right, sir. Now, just one final question. We know that in May, June, July, there are all sorts of things that are happening in Central Bosnia and you had indicated earlier, I believe it was to one of the questions asked by the Bench that the situation was difficult and there were complaints. Could you please tell us how difficult was that situation knowing that you have Croats that are now coming as refugees along with Muslims that are coming as refugees and you have the fighting going on. Could you please give the Trial Chamber some indication of what is really happening, how difficult the situation is, because, after all, we need to have all of these events in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think you forgot to mention the year. You gave the months. 1993, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask the same thing but when you suggest 1993, I think it was during 1992 this man was in position, not in May, June, July 1993. He was no longer in that position so I assumed, I thought correctly, that Mr. Karnavas was talking about 1992 which is the focus of this man's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I don't mean to be -- we're not living in a bubble. The gentleman was there, was in Croatia, and I can paint a picture for the Court. Imagine seeing people getting killed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we don't need a long speech. It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's my whole point --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We want -- Mr. Karnavas wants to make another speech. Your Honour, I submit to the Chamber the Chamber has heard the testimony of this witness. The Chamber knows the Prosecution's been quite transparent about its position on this timing and it's not appropriate for this witness, this person, to give evidence concerning about these detailed matters or any such things when he was not in that position. And we've made no secret of that. I simply want the Chamber to have fair evidence and this witness has talked about the period up to March 1993 and then he comes back later in 1995. Yes. He may have had some limited ongoing connection but this witness has never testified, has never testified since yesterday about any extensive involvement in these matters in mid-1993 and I do object. There's no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard very briefly on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be -- if I may be heard, Your Honour, just for the sake -- because he was living in Croatia, he's in the situation. He can see it. I'm asking him as a human being as someone who was over there. If I may be allowed -- we're hearing comments from the peanut gallery now. If I may be allowed to make my comment for the record. He is there. You can take it for whatever weight you wish but he is there. I'm not asking him the situation in the camps, but in general, the atmosphere. Is this gentleman not capable of commenting in general about the atmosphere in Croatia, be it dealing with the politics, dealing with the transitional period? Of course. Now we're talking about huge amounts of refugees coming from both sides and I'm asking him to give us his impression from his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please rephrase your question, and that will be your last question since your time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please describe to us the situation, the atmosphere of what it was like to be in Croatia at that period of time, May, June, July, August, when you had Croats being driven out in Central Bosnia when the conflict was occurring and Croatia is absorbing refugees both that are Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't easy to live in Croatia at that time. We also received reports about massacres committed against Croats and it wasn't easy to stay aloof. Many people, including members of the Croatian parliament and myself tried to go there and did indeed go there. I went to Central Bosnia on several occasions and with all due respect to everybody present, I didn't see any of you there. I was there. And we tried to establish some links, open channels of communication, reach members of the BiH parliament. And I was successful on one occasion. I led a delegation of my fellow MPs to Nova Bila which is a village in Central Bosnia. Croatia had donated the funds to build a hospital there. It was built and as the highest-ranking official, I was supposed to lay the foundation for it and apart from Croatian officials, we also invited representatives from Zenica, Doboj and other places under Bosnian Muslim control to the ceremony. I'm mentioning this as an example. I asked the colleagues to take me to Bugojno because it was practically impossible to go there so I was taken there by Bosnian Muslims and they, in return, asked me to take them Kiseljak because it was impossible for them to go there and we asked them to take us to Vares because without their help it wasn't possible for us. And they asked me to take them to the part of Vitez that was off limits for them and we did all that and talked to the people and tried to set up channels of communication. Eventually, we went to Mostar and I enabled them to have talks on the western side and they and Mr. Kosnik who was the international -- who was the international manager, the military officer in charge enabled them to cross to the other side so we were crossing front lines and that was dangerous but I believe that such activities contributed to putting an end to the conflict.
