We lived in such circumstances and we tried to do something to bring about peace and enable people to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the period of this, so we have a framework? What period, especially with Nova Bila because there are allegations that are allegations that we're trying to ethnically cleansing -- reverse ethnic cleansing of the Croats and now you're talking about building a hospital there.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was around about the signing of the Washington Agreement, I believe that was in the fall of 1994, probably or 1995. I believe it was in 1994. Yes, why should we have invested so much money, so much of our own money in the construction of a hospital and we also had people in Zagreb and Split to receive training and specialist training and that hospital is still open. There are ethnic Croats and Bosnian Muslims working there -- doctors, I mean, and there are also other medical facilities specialised for the respective activities and I believe that the existence of this hospital in Central Bosnia is the best evidence for Croatia's wish for the people to stay there and return there. I remember that a stone that weighed several tons was taken there from Zagreb cathedral and we -- it bears an inscription saying that it is the Croatian wish for the people who had been wounded to stay there and live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate your honesty and your forthrightness in answering all of my questions and if you would be so kind to do the same with my colleagues and questions that come from the Prosecution or from the Bench. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the cross-examination, how are we going to deal with the other accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will need some 15 to 20 minutes to deal with two topics. I don't believe I will need more. And Ms. Alaburic may need a little more than that. The other Defence counsels, as far as I know, have not expressed a wish to interrogate the witness. [In English] I would kindly ask assistance of the usher to distribute some documents. [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind the Chamber's guidelines in the ruling dated the 24th of April, 2008, my examination can be classified as cross-examination. I will refer to subjects that have been broached in a way but I do believe that there are some remaining details that merit further examination. By your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Kovacic, I defend General Praljak. I thank you for your willingness to testify. I would like to ask you the following question: You worked in Croatia at the time in question between March 1993 and late 1995, you were an MP. You said that at page 20, lines 10 through 14 of yesterday's transcript. The first question that I would like to ask you is this, or rather, to speed things along a little, you've been handed the bundle of documents. Can you please look at the second document in that bundle. The number is 3D 01092. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have a look. It should be easy enough for you to recognise, this is a diplomatic note dispatched by Croatia's foreign ministry on the 30th of April, 1993, to the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb in order to notify them of the desire by a multi-party parliamentary delegation of Croatia to visit Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you go to the second paragraph of that document, the purpose of that visit is defined. At the time, you were an MP. We are looking at the 30th of April, 1993. Are you aware of this parliamentary delegation? Why was it set up? Why did they want to go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, this is about what was going on in Bosnia, specifically Central Bosnia. At the time, this was a foremost concern in political terms in Croatia. I'm aware of this initiative. This, I believe, was the first time ever that a parliamentary delegation like this visited this neighbouring country. They wanted to go there and see for themselves what precisely was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do you know or do you remember any specifics as to what had preceded this decision by the parliament to dispatch this delegation and how did that come about? Who brought this about? Can you tell us anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was prompted by the development over there. The excuse, as it were, for this was as follows: Mr. Praljak, one fine day, turned up in front of the parliament and he started lobbying with the delegate. I think there were other people with him but the -- he is quite a striking character and his physical appearance is difficult to forget. He stood out in that group and he was talking to the delegates out in the hall. "It's nice to be in Zagreb. There are lots of stories being bandied about, some of which are simply untrue. Please go there, see for yourselves what's going on and help us put a stop to it." Roughly speaking, that was, in my understanding, the gist of what he was trying to say. This was followed by a session of the delegates. One of the conclusions that was reached was to set up a multi-party parliamentary delegation to visit those areas. Upon their return, they were to submit a report. I think this was the course of action that was eventually taken. Some of the areas were reached with the assistance of international agents and international organisations had been informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript to be perfectly clear, you say Praljak was lobbying about them needing to go over there or down there. When you say "down there," I suppose that's a reference to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the assistance of the international forces bearing in mind of course the situation that prevailed on the ground at the time, the checkpoints, the war that was going on, the checkpoints along the roads and so on and so forth. Can you please look at document number 2. This is 3D 00566. It's a letter signed by Ivo Sanader, at the time Croatia's deputy foreign minister. Again, we see the header, the stamp Republic of Croatia Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was sent to General Wahlgren who, at the time, was the UNPROFOR commander at the time. Is this document consistent with what you actually know, that the assistance of the international forces had been requested?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wahlgren at the time was the commander of all the international forces and the foreign ministry asked for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we look at both these documents, they both tell us who exactly the delegation comprised, a total of seven persons. I'm not reading their names now, it's not entirely necessary. You see the parentheses there and -- but their party affiliations are specified as well. It is quite clear that we are looking at a multi-party delegation including representatives of all the political parties and can you tell the Court, the Court knows what the HDZ is, I think that has been addressed sufficiently. They know who HSLS are, and the SDP and the other parties.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a multi-party delegation. Three members of the ruling party, the remaining persons belonging to opposition parties, a total of four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. More on this, if you could just look at the last document in my binder, 3D 01091. 3D 01091. Look at the title and look at the introduction. That will suit my purpose for the time being. It's a report of the multi-party parliament delegation of national assembly, the Republic of Croatia on the mission of goodwill in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can all read the first paragraph so I'm not reading it out loud. Is this the delegation that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the delegation that I was talking about except for the fact that one of the representatives of the ruling party was replaced, he was away on business somewhere and he was replaced by someone else but this is the same delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not going any further into these reports. It is apparent they had meetings over there. They had talks. They are specific about the detail of those talks. Just for the sake of the transcript, all these three documents for the benefit of the Chamber have already been admitted into evidence. Let me just go back to General Praljak's lobbying. What you said a while ago. You told us what you thought was the gist of that. Do you, perhaps, remember whether General Praljak was given a chance to address the parliament directly to address the delegates concerning this discussion that was going on at the time, about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the possibilities of an improvement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about that. I belonged to a different chamber. This was a chamber of delegates so we are looking at a different section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. That was what I was going to confirm. Unless I'm wrong, you were the member of the county chamber; right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this was for the delegates; right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So logically --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please be asked to speak one at a time. Thank you very much. The interpretation will then proceed.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop. There seems to be a problem, a technical problem. Can you resume your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember Mr. Praljak. I remember him from the lobby of the parliament. I remember him -- seeing him in the press room and outside the parliament too. He's easy to spot. He is very direct when he speaks and he is very outspoken. Not a difficult man to notice. It was a surprise for me when I first set eyes on there but he was very graphic about he was asking people to do. He didn't mince his words. He said, "Go over there, see for yourself what's going on." That was the gist of what he was telling people. I can't remember who else was with him. There were other people with him at the time but I can't remember who specifically. I am sure he was the one who played the principal role in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I think that's sufficient and we can now move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next subject that I wanted to raise with you is this. This is something that was brought up several times during your chief. First of all, you mentioned yourself that you visited Bosnia-Herzegovina several times back in 1994 and 1995 on humanitarian convoys. This is just to assist others. The transcript reference, yesterday's transcript this is page 79, lines 19 through 22. Today, towards the close of your examination in chief, page 45, you mentioned a visit to Bosnia, that parliamentary group. Therefore, the visit that we've been discussing so far, that was the first one and others followed; right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, this was the first one and other visits followed at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just for the transcript, we have to wait and avoid overlapping. Okay. Let's move on to something else now. Towards the end of your cross today, I think that's page 45 and there was something at page 21 and page 22, I think you mentioned something about soldiers, BH army soldiers who, in some cases, individuals even visited their families in Croatia. Bearing in mind your job in the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons but also your position in the parliament, I'm sure you were following the situation and you knew what was going on. Sir, is it true that there were soldiers of the BH army who were being accommodated in various medical institutions in Croatia, in hospitals and rehabilitation centres?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case throughout the war and this particularly applied to Split hospital. They were admitting on a permanent basis many wounded members of the BH army but it also applied to some extent to Zagreb's hospital such as Rebro and the new hospital. Many of them underwent surgery and were then moved on to rehabilitation centres, just like anyone else. I think we're looking at quite a large number of people. I wasn't following this situation very closely but I know there are reports that were written about this and I know that many of them were provided this type of medical assistance with a focus on Split hospital. I think they have in-depth documents, they have case histories of each and every patient that was treated at the hospital back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We need to make a pause. Nevertheless, I'm really looking to get something else from you about what was going on, another aspect of this situation. These patients obviously are also receiving visits from family members, from neighbours, from people from their home village. Were there refugees in Croatia also at the time, were you aware of cases such as those?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned this in a way, but let me raise this: Those people both the refugees and the soldiers who were in hospitals, they were watching Croatian TV, reading Croatian newspapers, they were just there. And they watched the TV and they see their own side winning or losing over in Bosnia; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. We had cases, for example, where people within the same facility were at the same time rejoicing and weeping about the fate of their family members. I witnessed a situation like that and it really shattered me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This was a complex situation. It would be best, perhaps, to cite a number of examples to illustrate what exactly was going on. You mentioned something about witnessing a situation like that yourself. Can you please tell us more about it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about a facility near Makarska, an accommodation facility with refugees from Central Bosnia. There were both groups there. I'm talking about a family of a friend of mine who was a native of Vitez, his family was there. They had lost a number of their relatives. There were some other people who were also there at the time who had just caught wind of news that pleased them, that was in a way favourable. This was a difficult situation and they addressed me, they came to speak to me and asked me to move them elsewhere. It was in situations such as these that it was very difficult to expect that people such as these should be kept together. I put in a word for them and asked them to be moved to a different facility. I asked for the Croats to be moved to a different facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your background in terms of education, could we perhaps say that incidents such as these gave rise not just to political problems but also to social problems, if you like, that there were ethical issues at stake? Issues regarding human behaviour, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right. It's very give to keep your presence of mind in situations such as these but it is at the same time indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have information on an incident in a hospital in Dalmatia. There was another scene such as the one you just described, someone won and someone lost and then there was some wounded Bosnian soldiers around who sang for joy when they had heard something, some news that pleased them. This led to an incident. This was sometime in the summer of 1993. Were you aware of this particular one or were you aware of perhaps other such incidents involving the same type of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this specific one but I am aware of there having been incidents such as the one you've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be given a chance, Your Honours, to ask a single question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one. Why? Prompted by what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clarification. Clarification of this situation. We are sort of beating about the bush and I would like to ask a more direct question regarding the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to discuss with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you something you did not answer. My colleagues are asking what the reason could be for a question put by you based on the guidelines we issued, namely, that you would have a personal technical knowledge of the issue, that you may have met with the witness. On what grounds would you be authorised to ask a question since that was the decision by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I need is to shed some light on the situation, it goes like this. There were refugees in Croatia in 596 different places in terms of there being facilities that were specifically set up. Very often Croats and Bosniak Muslims were together. Incidents occurred in places such as those. To my knowledge, incidents were like this and I'd like to ask the witness whether he knows anything about that. There were places where Bosniaks were celebrating certain victories of the BH army over the Croats and this constituted unpleasant behaviour on their part. So that is the gist of my question. Were there celebrations going on whenever important victories were won by the BH army in Central Bosnia, were these celebrations going on in refugee centres across Croatia and how did the Croats who came from the same villages and were in the same refugee centres view these celebrations. It's a simple enough question. Once that is done, Your Honours, I would like to be given the floor to address the Court about my right to conduct examinations. I remember your ruling and your ruling states clearly if having special or personal knowledge, may I therefore please be allowed to address the Court to find out exactly how far the restrictions imposed on me would go and will it be within the Court's discretion every time to potentially compromise my right to a fair trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. There are two problems. The first problem is that you want to ask a question of the witness. We're going to discuss this first issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you wanted to put a question. This is without any purpose because the witness already answered. He said that there were incidents, there had been incidents linked to various events, for instance, that event in Bugojno, that was an example. So he answered already. Therefore, your question would not be of any additional value. It is moot, and there is no reason why it should be asked. However, you wanted to address the Court and I'm going to ask my colleagues again as to our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, following this discussion amongst the Judges, the Trial Chamber recalls that it handed down a decision on the scope of the questions you are authorised to ask. This decision was confirmed, was affirmed by the Appeals Chamber. It was handed down during the Prosecution case. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the same system should apply to the stage of the Defence case. Of course you can always file a request in writing. The Trial Chamber, after it has heard the Prosecutor, will rule, and you can always ask for a certification for appeal. This is what I have to say. It is a decision by the Trial Chamber affirmed by the Appeals Chamber so your right to ask questions is no way restricted all the more so since your counsel could have further presented the issue you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the ruling never says technical issues. Can you please be more specific about the exact meaning of the words that you signed? As far as I understood, this regarded questions pertaining to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I do not have the decision in front of me and I don't have the translation into your language of the decision. If you have that translation, read it again, because in our minds, it was very clear. Technical issues such as gunfire, anything related to the army in which you have a personal technical knowledge, you are entitled to ask questions. As to a special knowledge you might have with regard to a witness and precisely I wanted to ask a question of this witness and then you were on your feet and you prevented me from asking the question. Depending on the answer provided by the witness, you could have then intervened. All this is set out in our decision. You challenged it and the Appeals Chamber affirmed the position by the Trial Chamber. And I remind you, you know this better than anyone. There was a discussion within the Trial Chamber, I was in favour of not restricting your right but my colleagues decided otherwise. There is a majority that handed down a decision and I have to comply with it. This decision was affirmed by the Appeals Chamber. The majority decision of the Trial Chamber was confirmed. That's all I can say. I can't say anything else. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think this is the time for us to go into the specifics. Your ruling is what it is and I think we have so far remained in full compliance, especially during the OTP case. We were in keeping with the ruling. It defines what it defines; however, I cannot but state that towards the end of the OTP case, the Chamber's interpretation of that ruling was gradually and little by little becoming more restrictive until the Chamber said it loud and clear, military matters alone in relation to Mr. Praljak. Well, that wasn't the spirit or indeed the letter of your decision dated May 2007. I'd propose we don't waste any more time on this now. I will be filing a motion for this ruling to be reviewed, which is also my right. There is another thing that I have to say for the sake of the transcript. Bearing in mind the progress of this entire issue, bearing in mind the reasonably comprehensive right that the accused was given at the outset to take part in the cross-examination of a witness to a very high degree, and given the ruling passed by the Chamber which took a more restrictive approach, I appealed this but the Appeals Chamber turned me away and said that the original ruling by the Trial Chamber should apply. Despite all of this, the ruling was being interpreted in a more restrictive manner and that's why I think it needs reviewing. As a lawyer, however, at the same time, I'm afraid and I will be open about this, of the possibility of another even more restrictive ruling being passed. I think the one that was passed in May last year, although I did not fully agree with it, at least makes sure that the accused enjoys a minimum of rights that he would enjoy in the run of the mill European proceedings. However, should there be increasingly a more restrictive interpretation of the ruling, and that is my theory, that that's what we see happening here, then we'll be running into more and more problems because we are turning the accused into an object of these penal proceedings, according to our theory, especially the continental law theory, he should be involved in the proceedings. Another matter altogether, of course, is if an accused wastes time by asking irrelevant questions. Were that the case, the Chamber would have every right to put a stop to any such malpractice and save more time from being wasted. I do, however, propose to bring this to a conclusion. As far as my contribution is concerned, we shall be filing a special submission raising all these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Praljak, your Defence lawyer explained to us that he is going to file a motion explaining his reasons and he is going to do that later. What did you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me add that according to your ruling, which I know very well, whenever I have special knowledge and when I'm involved, I am entitled to ask questions, not only about military matters, although such a crystal-clear question clearly refers to the right of leading an army only 20 kilometres away from such events. This is essential to my view of things. I'm not accused only of military actions. The indictment says that I am the connection between the Croatian part of the joint criminal enterprise and it doesn't say only military but also politically. And I'm not only a soldier, but in a way, I engaged myself almost to the point of forcing the Sabor delegation to go down there. And I remind you that it says if the individual was involved in the events or has a special knowledge. It isn't only general knowledge. It's also the frame -- prevailing frame of mind and everything else pertaining to the chaos down there. I ask you once again to allow me to ask the question to be crystally clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to talk about it. Witness, I wanted to ask you the following question. You've told us as an MP and we've learned that you were a member of the High Chamber whereas there's also the Chamber of Representatives. You have heard Mr. Praljak lobbying and we also know that you yourself have been there. You've been there because the counsel showed us some documents stating that other MPs went on the premises as well. So I wanted to ask you some questions before the intervention of Mr. Praljak. Do you personally know Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew him. He lived in Zagreb and I had known him since 1990 when he first stepped out into public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question: When you were in Central Bosnia, and we know that you were there during a period while -- where warring parties were warring, so to begin with, who were you taken care of, by the HVO or by the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never acted on the behalf of either one or the other side. We were always acting on our own behalf but we needed the assistance of both parties to reach some areas. We didn't have big problems with the HVO, but when we came as far as Prozor, for example, we often had to negotiate and seek contact with all parties to be let to pass through. And we involved everybody from who we expected assistance and we tried to make our stay there public because it was a sort of guarantee for our safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Amongst the contacts that you had, did you have a contact, for instance, with Mr. Praljak either in writing, on the phone, orally, through someone? Did he play a role so that you and your MPs were able to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in my particular case. He may have played a role but I'm unaware of it. Anyway, I didn't ask him for any such services or favours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So during your stay, you never had any contacts with Mr. Praljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. While he was in his position, while he led the HVO or whatever he did, I don't know, I'm not a military expert, he certainly was an important personality there, but I never had contact with him about these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, talking about the ABiH, who was your contact there? Who was your main contact in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were never able to reach high ranking people. We always negotiated with the local commanders or directly with the soldiers at checkpoints. Most times we had to speak with local commanders, and there were always many local commanders, and speak to the soldiers at the checkpoints themselves to let you pass. Sometimes they would do so; sometimes not. Sometimes they would order us to return or, then again, they would say, Wait until the situation calms down, et cetera. To us, the local commanders were always the most important people or their immediate superiors. I never contacted high level commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the introduction to this series of questions was linked to the mission of parliamentarians but you of course are speaking of other visits which you paid to Bosnia because you were not, as far as I can take from the documents, a member of the parliamentary delegations although you were an MP at the moment. Is that correct? Could you confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was indeed not a member of that delegation although I was an MP. This delegation left in an organised fashion, supported by international forces that had been notified, as well as the BiH embassy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for your answers. We are now going to give the floor to Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning -- good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zoric. My name is Vesna Alaburic and I am Defence counsel of Mr. Milivoj Petkovic. Tell me, did you know Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances in which you got to know him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got to know him through his career. He was a public personality and he was present in the media so I learned about him and on some occasions, we met in person but I cannot say I know him well. I know that he was a soldier and I know roughly what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good. I do not think I will need to speak to you long, but we need to clarify some details. You explained to us here that Croatia was a signatory to the International Convention on the Status of Refugees and to the protocol on the status of refugees from 1967, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croatia was indeed a signatory. The convention was from 1957, I believe, and the convention from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I recall what my learned friend Judge Prandler was going to say. Wait so the interpreters can translate the answer before you continue speaking because you were again overlapping to an extent that was hardly manageable even to these excellent interpreters that we have. I want to pay homage to them and support them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to confirm that I am of the same views, but I also would like to say that actually the Geneva Convention was concluded in 1951 and not in 1957. For the record I would like to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for these instructions which I hope we will follow. And thank you, Judge Prandler, for this correction. The witness stated correctly that the convention was from 1951 and the protocol from 1967.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, let us try and see when Croatia became a party to these international documents. Do you know that Croatia through the notification about succession from the first day of its independence on the 8th of October 1991, became a party to many international agreements including agreements on the status of refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that but Croatia, upon the request of the EU, suspended its declaration of independence for a period of three months but I think that under all international conventions of the UN, including the ones we've mentioned, that Croatia became a party to these conventions after it was admitted as a member of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My apologies to everybody in the courtroom, but, Mr. Zoric, I believe that you made an inadvertent mistake. Can we agree that Croatia declared its independence in July 1991, but the three months' suspension was proclaimed in July 1991 and that it expired in October 1991 so that we celebrate our day of independence in October 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that through the notifications on succession, the Republic of Croatia as from the first day of its independence became a party to these international agreements?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Good, I just wanted to clarify. Tell us, Mr. Zoric, do you know that international agreements under the Croatian constitution are part of the Croatian legal system, of course, provided that Croatia is a party to those agreements?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that under the Croatian constitution, such international agreements have greater force, take a priority over Croatian legislation, national legislation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that international legislation takes priority over national legislation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of a very important document which you discussed extensively with Mr. Karnavas. You needn't waste time looking for this document, it is document 1D 2626, and of the set of documents submitted by the Defence of Jadranko Prlic, under number 4, the dynamics of the refugee crisis, it is said that the Republic of Croatia was faced with a huge number of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina from the April of 1992 onwards. Can you confirm that this is correct? That from April 1992, Croatia was faced with a wave of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In three or four months only, the number rose by over 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, their exact data of this growth in April, there were already over 190.000; in August, over 360.000; in December, over 370.000 and so on. According to your knowledge, are these accurate data?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now together establish which regulation on refugees was in force when Croatia started to be faced with the wave of refugees. Please take a look at your set of documents. Document number 4D 1232. A remark to the Trial Chamber. The Law on the Movements and the Stay of Foreigners is not translated entirely but only up to Article 43 so I consider it necessary to refer to that piece of legislation to show how Croatia regulated the status of refugees. I do not intend to discuss individual provisions in any detail with the witness. Mr. Zoric, please take a quick look at Article 22 which speaks about the stay of foreigners based on the recognised status of refugees. And then the entire chapter 5, refugees, in other words, Articles 31 through 38, and there are other articles also. My question with regard to this is: Is it correct that getting the status of refugee in the Republic of Croatia was regulated by the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners which I have referred to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise in advance if I've missed it. Do we have an English translation of any of these materials? No. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. I am very sorry that the law is not translated in it's entirety. I announced yesterday that in my cross-examination, I would be referring to this law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Again you say in it's entirety. Can you point out the parts that are translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is translated up to and including Article 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I just wanted to help Ms. Alaburic and say that the law had been translated into English here and we find it here. And also, actually, in the very first part of it in Article 2, it refers to the refugees, the meaning of the refugees and also to the fact that it is being based on the 1951 Convention of the Status of Refugees and the 1957 Protocol on the Status of Refugees. I would add that that protocol was adopted in New York in the framework of the United Nations while -- whereas the 1951 Convention was adopted in Geneva by the states who participated in that diplomatic conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please, Ms. Alaburic. We have a problem. In your binder, we have the document 4.131. There's also the document 4D 1232. And that document is not translated. In other words, I don't have the translation in English of that particular document. So when you are mentioning section 22 and section 22 of which document? We don't have the translation in English and it's also not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may go on. What we have is the Law on Asylum but I suppose it's not the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in my set of documents, there are two laws. One is the Law on Asylum and the other is the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners. The Law on Asylum is translated into English. It was passed in 2003 and that law overruled some articles, some provisions of the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners which was passed in 1991, and the provisions overruled pertain to refugees. The law that I do not have translated is the latter-mentioned Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners. I said that I had an English translation of the first half of that law and if you want to establish that Chapter 5 indeed deals with the issue of refugees, I'm willing to put this document on the ELMO. I didn't deem that necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't know what you wish to highlight by putting these questions to the witness. If your questions are of paramount importance, then you have to make sure that the Judges have the English version of the text. How can we give a probative value of a text that we do not see, we don't have a translation of that text and you're going to present some fragments and portions of the text. This is what I don't understand. When you prepared the cross-examination of this witness and if you want to raise some very important points that could have an impact on us and this trial, please come to trial with translated documents. We -- you know what we are doing. We can look at the text from section 1 to the last section. We of course -- we're not sitting here with crossed arms and listening to you. We're sitting here but we're also looking at the document and I scanned the documents from back to back, in fact, so I scanned the document to see if you did not omit to mention something. But if you show me a document in your own language and if I cannot do my job, then all I have to do is just sit here with my arms crossed and wait for your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said right away that I do not intend to analyse laws with this witness who is not a lawyer by profession. I submitted this law for a simple reason. Yesterday, we spoke about the Law on the Status of Refugees and Displaced Persons and the Chamber asked a number of questions from which I concluded clearly that they do not understand based on which basis people from Bosnia-Herzegovina were granted the status of refugees because the law that had been submitted pertained only to citizens of the Republic of Croatia and events taking place in Croatia. It is my intention for this witness to say that the status of refugee was regulated in the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners. We have a -- the translation of half that law. I do not tender that into evidence because it isn't entirely translated but we intend to do so and then tender it into evidence. For the purposes of cross-examination, it suffices for this witness to say to you, Your Honours, that the -- getting the status of refugees for persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina was regulated by the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners. What is additionally important for me is to establish that this law was passed in June 1991, that it came into force on the 8th of October, 1991, namely on the day of -- when Croatia became independent. And now the issue I wanted to discuss with the witness whether, at the moment this law was passed, anybody expected that Croatia would be faced with such a refugee problem, refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was my intention to point out which law regulates what and then I can enable you to consult that legislation, if you deem it necessary, once it has been translated. You can see that I'm telling the truth in document 4D 1231, which is the Law on Asylum and which exists in an English translation, and in its final article, Article 72, it says which provisions of the Law on the Movement and Stay of Foreigners are being overruled by this new act and that these provisions pertain to refugees. This is all I considered necessary to state about this. So I just merely wanted to point out which Croatian legislation regulated these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must join the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Scott was on his feet before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I didn't see that. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I absolutely accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Your Honour, I will make clear at the outset I'm not raising the slightest question whatsoever about counsel's good faith or good intentions. There's no question about that in my mind at all. However, there is a fundamental problem here and that -- and again, I take counsel absolutely at her word but she's just represented to all of us in the courtroom that the very law that is not translated is apparently the law that she says applies despite after a day and a half of evidence and those of us in the courtroom who do not speak Croatian don't have that law available to us. I can't ask questions. I can't conduct cross-examination based on that and unless -- I mean, I don't want to read back but I think what counsel's told us in the last few minutes is that everything we've been talking about for the last day and a half, the status of refugees in Croatia is regulated by this law that we don't have a translation of. How can it possibly be more central than that? And I can't conduct -- I can't go forward and conduct a cross-examination when I don't have a document that I can work with. Again, I know it's difficult to prepare all these documents, the Prosecution faces the same situation, but I can't possibly go forward without a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also wish to join the Prosecution in their objection because I am entitled to redirect and if I understand Ms. Alaburic has indicated that we don't know what we're doing here. As you've noted, I've shown Dr. Rebic's letter which referred to the decision which was in the Official Gazette, the specific paragraphs which at least in Dr. Rebic's mind that was the law that applied. Also, if you look at the timing of it because after this, you have a decree then you have the decision. We heard why the decision was necessary. And so if Counsel Alaburic wishes to take us on, then I suggest that she provide us with an English translation. Far be it for me as a foreigner to discuss Croatian law; but as lawyer, I think I'm pretty capable of reading this and so is my colleague. And I would object to her characterisation that this was the law that applied versus the law that we showed, both the decree and the decision, especially given that Dr. Rebic refers to the decision in his letter and his answer to Ambassador Turkovic with respect to why certain individuals were being sent back to Bosnia-Herzegovina when it appeared, at least to Dr. Rebic, the situation there had calmed down and therefore they no longer enjoyed the status of refugees. So I would say unless we have an English version, I would object to any further questioning on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, this issue of the legal status of refugees is not a novel one. For months already or months ago, I can't remember which witness, it was I personally had said, asking this of the Defence, I'd asked them what were the legal instruments that were applicable in the Republic of Croatia governing the state of refugees. I myself had asked the question and I remember quoting the Geneva Conventions but I'd asked what was the applicable Croatian law. I'd raised the issue. That was months if not over a year ago. And today, you appear to say something which is fine, you may be right, I'm not saying that you're wrong, but then you have to come prepared with the translation into English of this law so that precisely the Judges may ask questions. The Prosecutor objected because he said that if he wants to cross-examine, he needs the text; and Mr. Karnavas has just said that he, too, wants to have that text in his language. So that's the situation as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I'd just like to offer an explanation. I was going to call my own witness to talk about refugees and the Law on the Status of Refugees by that time certainly would have been translated into English. It was because you raised the issue yesterday, not just because Judge Antonetti had raised the issue but also because of the kind of answer that Mr. Zoric provided when he said that it wasn't just the Decree on the Status of Refugees and Displaced Persons but rather that there were also regulations defining the status of all foreigners. I was preparing my cross-examination yesterday and I decided to ask the witness this question. I thought it would be fair to raise this law, to refer to it, invoke it, but I'm not going to delve any deeper into that; it was just a foundation for my next question. My next question is about the status of refugees and displaced persons which is something that was in force when he was still in office and the document is 1D 2588. This is in the set of documents handed to you by the Prlic Defence team. Can you please have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question is: Can we agree that this document was in force until October 1993 when a new law was passed, the one that you discussed yesterday when prompted by Mr. Karnavas? 2588.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at Article 26 that Mr. Karnavas invoked in relation to this law and the Article is contained in this provision, the provisions of Article 13 through 19 of this decree shall be applied in an appropriate way to refugees. Can we therefore agree that in Articles 13 through 19 of the decree what we see defined there is assistance for refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Articles 13 through 19 tell us about the sort of assistance that refugees would be provided. Article 26 says that both refugees and displaced persons should be treated in this same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So was this the legal basis for displaced persons in Croatia to be enjoying exactly the same rights as refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, those who left Bosnia and Herzegovina to go to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the legal foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to 1D 2626. I'll read the relevant portion for you so you don't waste any time looking for it. This is section 5, paragraph 5, it reads, "In Croatia there exists and there existed from the very outset of the humanitarian and refugee crisis a unified system under which one was looking after the refugees from both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina not discriminating based on their ethnicity. All refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of their ethnicity received the same treatment and same status." Mr. Zoric, can you confirm that this conclusion I just read out to you is accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The conclusion is accurate. If I may just be allowed to add a couple of words. Given the context that we're talking about, we often only discuss refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, be they Croats or Bosniaks or Muslims; however, over in Croatia, as statistics show, we had not a major amount of Serb refugees, but there were some Serb refugees and there were Jewish refugees who fled Sarajevo. They were part of Sarajevo's Jewish community. Therefore, if you asked me about my preference, we -- I would like to discuss persons who are refugees. It is not entirely necessary to talk about their ethnic background in purely humanitarian terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were our indictment not worded the way it is, to the effect that Croats were doing something to undermine the Muslims, I would be all too happy to agree with you. This way I have to talk about the various ethnicities. Over 360.000 people had already reached Croatia from B and H by August that year, refugees. Can you please go back to my set of documents. I'm talking about the agreement on cooperation dated the 21st of July, 1991, by Izetbegovic, President Izetbegovic and President Franjo Tudjman. Can we please look at item 3 of the agreement. This is P 0339. It's in my binder. It's a document that we've already seen quite often in courtroom. Paragraph 3 or Article 3 reads, I quote, "The state delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina expressed their gratitude to Republic of Croatia for admitting and absorbing refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to an extent that is far above its real potential, realistic potential or capacity." Mr. Zoric, did people from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina often express their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia because of the good care that was taken of their refugees in Croatia and because of the assistance that they were provided?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a single meeting occurring with President Izetbegovic without him repeating this over and over again. Therefore, any time there was a meeting, whenever there was a meeting with President Izetbegovic this was one of the topics that were raised and then gratitude was always expressed. It was always something that was an incentive and a very encouraging thing to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let -- it reads on, "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia are now facing the burning issue of mass expulsions, particularly of the Muslim and Croat populations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They will continue to cooperate in putting up refugees in the Republic of Croatia as well as in other countries. They will continue to cooperate in collecting the humanitarian aid for refugees. They will continue to build refugee centres in safe areas throughout B and H and they will continue to work on the return of refugees from the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For that purpose, a special protocol on cooperation will be signed." Mr. Zoric -- Mr. Zoric, can you tell us whether you know whether such a protocol on cooperation was signed?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, protocol on cooperation was signed and there were later protocols that dealt more with the return of refugees. The first ones were mostly about refugees being provided accommodations and assistance. I think the first protocols date back to the first half of 1995 that talk about cooperation in terms of the refugees being allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at 3D 2710 in my set of documents, this is a General Praljak Defence document, protocol on cooperation of the government of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on dealing with the problem of refugees from B and H. This was signed on the 22nd of July, 1992. It was signed by the following: The prime ministers, Franjo Greguric and Jure Pelivan. Can you look at the protocol, please, and they you can tell us whether this is the protocol that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the protocol that we've been talking about. It's a result of this agreement and one thing that I must point out is that if you look at who has signed this document, it says Franjo Greguric, who was then prime minister, but the signature actually belongs to his deputy Mate Granic, who, at the time, was in charge of business such as this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Article 4 of the protocol it says that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I regret that it seems to always fall to me. I would be happy to share the burden with anyone else in the courtroom but unless I'm the only one, I don't have an English translation of this exhibit. And if anyone else does see this, I mean, all kidding aside, I would appreciate not being the only one who has to raise these objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we run checks, we've checked the Praljak Defence documents and we ascertained that this was one of the documents that were still being translated. This is a document that has not been translated yet, therefore, it cannot be tendered. However, I don't think this constitutes a sufficient reason for us to not discuss this document right now. We can have it placed on the ELMO, if necessary, and then we can try to interpret any points that we deem necessary. All that I'm interested in right now is item 4. I will try to read it and then the interpreter can easily interpret this for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... would be faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Article 4 reads, "The government of the Republic of Croatia and the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall seek an increase in international aid from the international community especially as regards Bosnia and Herzegovina. It shall also ask for more refugees to be admitted by neighbouring European countries, refugees who it will not be possible to provide assistance for in Bosnia and Herzegovina itself. The republic, the government of the Republic of Croatia is not in a position to cover the costs of transport or indeed international humanitarian aid that is being shipped into Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zoric, based on this it would seem that the two governments spoke and they agreed to address Europe because the situation was this: There were more refugees coming and Croatia could no longer absorb these new refugees. They were now to be sent to third countries. Is my understanding of this protocol is correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think your understanding of this protocol is correct. The governments did meet. The Croatian government on the one hand and the Bosnian government on the other addressed European countries. It was something that was widely debated in international conferences that there was contact in progress about this and some European governments responded to this request. They came up with specific quotas in terms of how many refugees would be admitted ranging from Hungary, Austria, Germany to Italy, Denmark, the Netherlands, as well as a number of other European governments that I've been mentioning here. It was through the mediation of international organisations that they expressed their willingness to admit a certain number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. If we go back to Defence document -- Prlic Defence document 1D 2626, if you look at Article 4 of that document, paragraph 6 of Article 4 and I will read it to you. It reads: "Following an appeal that was launched by the government of the Republic of Croatia in July 1992 to countries of western Europe to admit and take in Bosnian refugees, a section of a huge refugee convoy from Bosnia and Herzegovina will be heading west through Croatia." This appeal that I'm referring to here, is that appeal in keeping with the protocol signed by the presidents or prime ministers of the two countries?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that appeal is perfectly in keeping with that protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now tell me this, we're talking about July, the middle of 1992. Mr. Zoric, sometime halfway through 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina, are there any armed clashes going on between Muslims and Croats, I think there were none; right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none had erupted by this time. At least none that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that the departure of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina for so-called third countries halfway through 1992 and at later stages as well by it's very nature could not have been a result of some clashes between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a perfectly logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This concludes my cross examination. I apologise yet again for having to use documents that have not been yet translated, but as I said, there was simply no other way to go around this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have completed your cross-examination. I think on the Defence side nobody else had any other questions which means that after the break, Mr. Scott, you can start your cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Nozica, is this the way things are going to unfold or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not off the mark, Your Honour. There is just one thing that I would like to raise before the break. This document that was used today in chief by Mr. Karnavas, the number being 1D 02626, is already an exhibit and the number is 2D 00486. Just a note to avoid confusion about this document being admitted. I think it will probably be used quite often and I think it's important to point this out now before we get into any further confusion surrounding this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translations -- the Judge's comments haven't been recorded. Well, anyway, I'll go ahead. Your Honour, I just wanted to make for the record just so, again, that there's no argument or waiver or why I didn't raise it before that in connection with Ms. Alaburic's examination and these other follow-up examinations, the Prosecution continues its opposition to leading and directive questions by the supplemental examinations. The Prosecution will be filing -- making a written submission on that and just lest someone comes back and says that we've waived that or didn't raise it, I'm going to make it clear that continues to be our position. But we will make a written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 20 minutes' time, we shall resume our proceedings and you'll have 45 minutes for the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, counsel, and Dr. Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, I'd like to jump straight away into the question of refugee status and I will tell you that I'm also going to be drawing back upon your testimony in the -- what we call the Tuta-Stela or Naletilic/Martinovic case. And you recognise the difference, do you not, between someone who is "a refugee" and someone who is a "displaced person." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I spoke a great deal about that yesterday, didn't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And further, you recognise and, in fact, in the Tuta case you said there was a "big difference" between someone who has "refugee status and someone being a foreigner." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what sort of difference you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that someone who has been granted refugee status has substantial number of rights, at least on paper, as opposed to someone who is only considered a foreigner in the country?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they both have the same rights but there could be other differences such as origin, language, ethnicity. In terms of rights, I believe they have the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, in your Tuta-Stela testimony, you testified that there was a "big difference" between refugee status and someone being a foreigner. If someone is a refugee, the country is "bound to provide him with accommodations, schooling for the children, medical treatments, and all the rest that is necessary so that such a person is taken care of for life." Of your testimony. Then went on to answer that, "A foreigner, that is a person in Croatia who does not have refugee status did not, does not have those rights." Now, are you giving a different answer today than you gave in the Tuta-Stela case?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the transcript in front of me so therefore I can hardly be expected to comment. A foreigner could be a tourist, a student, a businessman, a foreigner is a person who comes from another country. A refugee is a person also who comes from another country but a person who enjoys certain rights once their status as a refugee has been recognised. Therefore, there can be certain differences. There are certainly big differences between mere tourists and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point, Your Honour, if Mr. Scott will be referring to portions of the transcript from the previous testimony, I would respectfully request page and line. I do have it in front of me in anticipation of his cross and so if he could be so kind. I'm sure he's going to quote accurately just so I can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. For the record I was just now referring to the testimony of the witness at page 11018 of his previous sworn testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you did say there that it was a "big difference" and I take it you've now modified your initial answer today to say, well, yes, in fact there are differences, refugees have rights, foreigners do not. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreigners have rights too, but they don't have the rights that refugees have. Regardless of that, I don't see why I should change what I said before about this. I think what I said before is consistent with what I'm saying now. I'm using plain language to put my point across, I'm not using legalese and I'm speaking in colloquial terms and my understanding is time is a valuable commodity in this courtroom. I'm trying to keep my answers short. What I said then I would say today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zoric. Let me be very clear then and I'm trying to be fair to you as well so let me be very transparent. I, for these purposes, am not going to be speaking generically or broadly. When I'm going to use the word "refugee" for purposes of my cross-examination, other counsel can do what they wish, but when I talk to you this afternoon and probably tomorrow, when I use the word "refugee," I'm talking about someone who has been granted refugee status under Croatian law. That's what I'm talking about, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we agree on that, Dr. Zoric?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it assists. Perhaps the -- it may save time. The ambiguity perhaps, at least to me, appears to stem not from refugee but what is meant by rights. Of course there are rights conferred under the Criminal Code, the Penal Code, and there are peculiar specific rights conferred by the Geneva Convention on Refugees, and, Your Honours, perhaps if one is specific on the question to what type of rights one is talking about, we may get clarity on the issue and no confusion. I don't know if it helps my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. That could be a source of confusion. If it is, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm speaking specifically in the context of refugees and I'll just simply, again, use your own words when you testified previously on page 11017 that if someone who has been granted a refugee status, the country granting that status is "bound to provide him with accommodations, schooling for the children, medical treatment, and all the rest that is necessary so that such a person is taken care of for life." Those are the rights I'm talking about now. And someone who is not a refugee, who has not been granted refugee status, does not have those rights. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone who has not been granted refugee rights could enjoy the right to an education or to receive assistance in some country. There were people in Croatia who did not have refugee rights but they were entitled to an education and especially to medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's again, as one of my colleagues likes to say, let's proceed then step by step and I'm talking now about perhaps some kind soul in Croatia gave them food, provided for some educational benefit, I'm talking now about the law of the state of the Republic of Croatia. And while someone might have given someone some benefit, a person who was from outside the country who was in Croatia who was not the granted the status of a refugee did not have the legal right, under Croatian law, to, as you said again, "... accommodation, schooling for the children, medical treatment, and all the rest that is necessary so that such a person is taken care of for life."

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a foreigner in Croatia and this foreigner is a refugee, then pursuant to the laws envisaging the answers to these questions, they would be receiving assistance. What happens in other countries other than Croatia, I mean, they might have different regulations with greater or lesser privileges. But it's also --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me cut across you because, as you say, time is precious, and if I'm not being clear, I apologise to you. My questions now are -- I'm talking about the Republic of Croatia. Several times now, you've given answers to what happens in other countries, you can't say. For the moment, with all due respect, sir, I don't care about any other country. I'm talking about the Republic of Croatia. You are also going in circles because a moment ago when you just answered, "If we have a foreigner in Croatia and this foreigner is a refugee ..." that begs the question, sir, you can have foreigners in Croatia, physically in Croatia that have not been granted refugee status under the law; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which exact foreigners do you mean? Can you explain? Do you mean foreigners who came to Croatia, asked for that status but weren't granted it or foreigners who came to the sea side? I don't know which ones you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Zoric, we've been talking since yesterday for some hours now about refugees and displaced persons. I'm not talking about tourists. If a person from Bosnia and Herzegovina during wartime conditions arrived in the state of Croatia and for whatever reason was not granted refugee status, was not considered a "refugee" and I told you a moment ago, when I say refugee, I'm talking about someone who's been granted legal status as a refugee under Croatian law, if they are not granted that status then they do not have the rights that you previously listed yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons who have been granted refugee status who, due to the wartime activities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and came to Croatia all have the same rights but in Croatia at the time, there were also persons who did not have that status. Fortunately, not all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been affected by the war so that there were areas from which people came for other reasons but didn't have refugee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll continue on for a moment and see if we can come at this maybe a slightly different way. Maybe you can assist the Chamber with this, just as a point of general information before we continue. I understand, based on what you've said before, that in the beginning, approximately 70 per cent of the refugees or -- excuse me, let's say to avoid confusion. In the beginning, 70 per cent of the persons coming from BiH under these conditions were Muslims. This later changed to approximately 50/50 Croat/Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The first refugees to arrive in Croatia were from eastern Bosnia and from around Prijedor. The arrival of refugees corresponded to the development of military activities either immediately preceding the activities or during those activities. There was an especially extensive arrival of refugees after cease-fire agreements had been signed because most towns only then civilians were willing to leave. So the refugees who had first arrived in Croatia were mostly Bosnian Muslims but then the proportions changed due to the events in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And further, it is correct, is it not, that of the total -- of these total persons coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina, approximately half came from what might be described as Serb-controlled areas, parts of the country, and about half came from areas controlled at that time by either the so-called Croat or Muslim sides? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is precise data about that, although from a military point of view, it may be necessary to scrutinise which territory was controlled by which forces. But -- people even coming from areas controlled by the ABiH could be refugees. Due to the harsh conditions and being afraid of shells coming from areas controlled by their forces, they were also refugees and we were unable to establish precisely those boundaries or delimitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So the answer to my question is approximately half came from Serb-controlled areas and approximately half came from Croat or Muslim areas; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At certain periods, that might apply, I'm not sure about which periods we are talking. But precise data can be found in reports submitted to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, what I just quoted you is what was your testimony in the Tuta-Stela case at page 10973. Now, we can agree and I think everyone in the courtroom has agreed over these past two days that by the spring, then, the late spring of 1992, the situation with persons coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina was such that Croatia was already running out or had run out of accommodation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We constantly had problems with accommodation because even the accommodation we had was deteriorating in quality with time due to the long stay of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct -- isn't it correct, sir, that on the -- because of those -- at least in part because of those conditions, that situation, on about the 13th of July, 1992, Croatia announced that it would not accept any more refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of giving them, as I said, "refugee status"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, Croatia made public that our resources are fully exhausted and the government appealed to international organisations to become more involved in this problem. After receiving aid and additional capacities, we continued granting refugee status to everybody who could meet the conditions for that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you -- you should have a binder there, sir, which should be tabbed in a similar fashion to the exhibits that you were looking at for the Prlic Defence and others, perhaps. If I could ask you, please, to turn to P 10406. I hope that they've all been provided to everyone in the courtroom at this point. P 10406. If you look behind it, sir, you should be able to find a Croatian language version. If you don't have it, please let me know. On the topic that I just raised with you a moment ago, this is an article from the Reuters news service dated the 13th of July, 1992. Starting off with the statement, "Croatia said on Monday it would not accept any more refugees from war-torn Bosnia-Herzegovina." If we go in the English version it's the first line on the second page, but I'm not sure about in the Croatian language, sir, but if you scan down the article, you will see, I believe, your name, "Damir Zoric, senior secretary of Croatia's Committee for refugees said funds and supplies were scarce. 'It is unbearable,' he told Reuters. 'It is not a question of good will. We don't have anywhere to put these people.'" And then at the end of the article it concludes with this, "The government statement said that refugee camps would now serve only as transit centres and that the new ruling would be enforced by the interior ministry." Now, does the situation as reported in this Reuters article, is that an accurate description of the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR ZORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I stated correctly that the situation was unbearable, if I understand English well enough, and that it isn't our good will that is the problem, but we have nowhere to put those people.
